Mark — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Mark was the nephew of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10) and the son of Mary of Jerusalem, whose house was a gathering place for the apostles and early Christians (Acts 12:12).

Because Peter called Mark his son (1 Peter 5:13), it is thought that Mark was converted through Peter's ministry.

Mark was thus closely associated with the disciples of Jesus, even if he had not personally been one of them.

He wrote in Rome.

Some suppose Peter dictated the Gospel to him. Henry considers it more generally attested, however, that Peter preached in Rome and that Mark, his companion, understood his preaching accurately and was asked to write down its details.

Peter's own humility is evident in the passages that mention him.

Mark's careful account includes many events Peter personally witnessed, and the details suggest the testimony of an eyewitness.

The Gospel emphasizes Christ's miracles more than his teaching discourses.

Though it repeats many events found in Matthew, reading them again is valuable: each evangelist records the events from the perspective that most affected him.

John prepares the Lord's way (verses 1–8)

Both Isaiah and Malachi spoke of the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ through the ministry of John the Baptist.

Their prophecies show that Christ comes among us with both a treasury of grace and a scepter of government.

Human corruption puts up great resistance to his progress.

When the Father sent his Son into the world, he prepared a way before him. When he sends Christ into a human heart, he likewise prepares the way.

John considered himself unworthy of the humblest service to Jesus.

The greatest saints have always been the most humble. They recognize their need of Christ's atoning blood and sanctifying Spirit more deeply than others.

The gospel promises people who repent and receive forgiveness that they will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, purified through his grace and refreshed through his consolations.

Often we gain little profit or comfort from God's ordinances, word and sacraments because we lack the divine light within us.

And we lack that light because we have not asked for it, though our heavenly Father promises to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

Jesus is baptized and tempted (verses 9–13)

Christ's baptism was his first public appearance after living unnoticed for many years.

How much genuine worth can remain unknown in this world!

Yet what is hidden will, at the appropriate time, be revealed.

Jesus took upon himself the likeness of sinful human flesh and consecrated himself for our sake so that we might become holy and be baptized with him (John 17:19).

The Father honored his submission to baptism. The Holy Spirit descended upon him like a dove.

Heaven may be said to open to us whenever the Spirit descends and works within us.

The good work God carries out in our hearts is evidence of his favorable purposes toward us.

Mark mentions that Jesus was in the wilderness among wild animals.

Even there his Father preserved him, encouraging confidence that the Father would continue providing whatever was necessary.

Special acts of protection give assurance of further help when it is needed.

The serpent tempted the first Adam in a garden and the second Adam in a wilderness, with very different outcomes.

He has continued tempting Adam's children in every place and condition.

Company has temptations; so does solitude.

No location, occupation or lawful activity is free from them—not even fasting and prayer.

Indeed, some of the fiercest assaults occur during sacred duties, yet through God's grace those duties also provide the sweetest victories.

The ministry of good angels comforts us against the malicious plans of evil angels.

But an even greater consolation is God the Holy Spirit living in our hearts.

Jesus preaches and calls disciples (verses 14–22)

Jesus began preaching in Galilee after John was imprisoned.

When God sets aside one servant, he raises up others to continue his work.

Jesus joined repentance and faith in his message.

Through repentance we acknowledge the Creator whom we have offended.

Through faith we honor the Redeemer who came to save us from sin.

Christ joined these two things; we must not separate them.

He called fishermen, people of modest worldly status who were diligent in their work and treated one another kindly.

Industry and unity are good, and Jesus delights to bless them.

Christ's followers must be willing to leave everything for his sake.

His grace makes them willing.

This does not mean everyone must literally withdraw from society.

Rather, we must hold worldly possessions and relationships loosely, giving up anything inconsistent with duty to Jesus or harmful to our souls.

Jesus faithfully observed the Sabbath by doing the spiritual and charitable work for which Sabbath rest was appointed.

His doctrine continually astonished people. The more carefully we hear it, the more reason we have to admire it.

Jesus casts out an unclean spirit (verses 23–28)

The devil is described as unclean because he has lost the purity of his original state, acts in direct opposition to God's Holy Spirit and makes human hearts impure through his suggestions.

Some people quietly attend gatherings where teachers offer only formal religion.

But when Christ comes through faithful ministers, holy doctrine and the convicting Spirit, they resist the truth and want no part in Jesus.

The unclean spirit in this story recognized Jesus as the Holy One of God.

It feared his holiness and expected destruction from him, rather than salvation.

People who tell God to depart from them speak the language of the same hostility.

The natural mind is opposed to God, particularly his holiness.

When Christ delivers souls from Satan's power, the change may produce turmoil.

The enemy tries to disturb people whom he can no longer destroy.

The witnesses wondered at the power of Jesus' teaching.

Equally astonishing changes occur when people become genuinely converted.

If we did not treat conversion with indifference, the transformation of a notoriously wicked person into a sober, righteous and godly life through preaching the crucified Savior would still astonish us.

Jesus heals many people (verses 29–39)

Wherever Jesus went, he did good.

He healed people so that they could serve him and others who belonged to him.

People prevented from attending public worship by illness or another genuine obstacle may still look for his gracious presence.

He can soothe their sorrow and reduce their pain.

The sick came in large numbers.

When we see others receiving help from Christ, it should encourage us to seek him ourselves.

Jesus withdrew to a solitary place.

He had no danger of pride or distraction, yet still sought time apart for prayer.

People who do the greatest amount of useful public work must also sometimes be alone with God.

Jesus cleanses a person with leprosy (verses 40–45)

The leper came to Christ with deep humility and full submission to his will.

“Lord, if you are willing” was not a question about Christ's compassion or power.

It was an expression of readiness to accept his decision.

We should pray with the same humility and trust.

Christ willingly shows mercy to people who willingly entrust their requests to his will.

He did not want this healing to become a means of attracting human praise for himself.

However, we have no such reason today to hesitate to proclaim Christ's praises.
classic_reading:
[Mark.1.1-Mark.1.8]
Mark
Mark was a sister's son to Barnabas, [Col.4.10] Col 4:10; and [Acts.12.12] Ac 12:12 shows that he was the son of Mary, a pious woman of Jerusalem, at whose house the apostles and first Christians assembled. From Peter's styling him his son, [1Pet.5.13] 1Pe 5:13, the evangelist is supposed to have been converted by that apostle. Thus Mark was closely united with the followers of our Lord, if not himself one of the number. Mark wrote at Rome; some suppose that Peter dictated to him, though the general testimony is, that the apostle having preached at Rome, Mark, who was the apostle's companion, and had a clear understanding of what Peter delivered, was desired to commit the particulars to writing. And we may remark, that the great humility of Peter is very plain where any thing is said about himself. Scarcely an action or a work of Christ is mentioned, at which this apostle was not present, and the minuteness shows that the facts were related by an eye-witness. This Gospel records more of the miracles than of the discourses of our Lord, and though in many things it relates the same things as the Gospel according to St. Matthew, we may reap advantages from reviewing the same events, placed by each of the evangelists in that point of view which most affected his own mind.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The office of John the Baptist. | (1-8) |
The baptism and temptation of Christ. | (9-13) |
Christ preaches and calls disciples. | (14-22) |
He casts out an unclean spirit. | (23-28) |
He heals many diseased. | (29-39) |
He heals a leper. | (40-45) |
Verses 1-8
Isaiah and Malachi each spake concerning the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, in the ministry of John. From these prophets we may observe, that Christ, in his gospel, comes among us, bringing with him a treasure of grace, and a sceptre of government. Such is the corruption of the world, that there is great opposition to his progress. When God sent his Son into the world, he took care, and when he sends him into the heart, he takes care, to prepare his way before him. John thinks himself unworthy of the meanest office about Christ. The most eminent saints have always been the most humble. They feel their need of Christ's atoning blood and sanctifying Spirit, more than others. The great promise Christ makes in his gospel to those who have repented, and have had their sins forgiven them, is, they shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost; shall be purified by his graces, and refreshed by his comforts. We use the ordinances, word, and sacraments without profit and comfort, for the most part, because we have not of that Divine light within us; and we have it not because we ask it not; for we have his word that cannot fail, that our heavenly Father will give this light, his Holy Spirit, to those that ask it.
[Mark.1.9-Mark.1.13]
Verses 9-13
Christ's baptism was his first public appearance, after he had long lived unknown. How much hidden worth is there, which in this world is not known! But sooner or later it shall be known, as Christ was. He took upon himself the likeness of sinful flesh; and thus, for our sakes, he sanctified himself, that we also might be sanctified, and be baptized with him, [John.17.19] Joh 17:19. See how honourably God owned him, when he submitted to John's baptism. He saw the Spirit descending upon him like a dove. We may see heaven opened to us, when we perceive the Spirit descending and working upon us. God's good work in us, is sure evidence of his good will towards us, and preparations for us. As to Christ's temptation, Mark notices his being in the wilderness and that he was with the wild beasts. It was an instance of his Father's care of him, which encouraged him the more that his Father would provide for him. Special protections are earnests of seasonable supplies. The serpent tempted the first Adam in the garden, the Second Adam in the wilderness; with different success indeed; and ever since he still tempts the children of both, in all places and conditions. Company and conversation have their temptations; and being alone, even in a wilderness, has its own also. No place or state exempts, no business, not lawful labouring, eating, or drinking, not even fasting and praying; often in these duties there are the most assaults, but in them is the sweetest victory. The ministration of the good angels is matter of great comfort in reference to the malignant designs of the evil angels; but much more does it comfort us, to have the indwelling of God the Holy Spirit in our hearts.
[Mark.1.14-Mark.1.22]
Verses 14-22
Jesus began to preach in Galilee, after that John was put in prison. If some be laid aside, others shall be raised up, to carry on the same work. Observe the great truths Christ preached. By repentance we give glory to our Creator whom we have offended; by faith we give glory to our Redeemer who came to save us from our sins. Christ has joined these two together, and let no man think to put them asunder. Christ puts honour upon those who, though mean in this world, are diligent in their business and kind to one another. Industry and unity are good and pleasant, and the Lord Jesus commands a blessing on them. Those whom Christ calls, must leave all to follow him; and by his grace he makes them willing to do so. Not that we must needs go out of the world, but we must sit loose to the world; forsake every thing that is against our duty to Christ, and that cannot be kept without hurt to our souls. Jesus strictly kept the sabbath day, by applying himself unto, and abounding in the sabbath work, in order to which the sabbath rest was appointed. There is much in the doctrine of Christ that is astonishing; and the more we hear it, the more cause we see to admire it.
[Mark.1.23-Mark.1.28]
Verses 23-28
The devil is an unclean spirit, because he has lost all the purity of his nature, because he acts in direct opposition to the Holy Spirit of God, and by his suggestions defiles the spirits of men. There are many in our assemblies who quietly attend under merely formal teachers; but if the Lord come with faithful ministers and holy doctrine, and by his convincing Spirit, they are ready to say, like this man, What have we to do with thee, Jesus of Nazareth! No disorder could enable a man to know Jesus to be the Holy One of God. He desires to have nothing to do with Jesus, for he despairs of being saved by him, and dreads being destroyed by him. See whose language those speak, that say to the Almighty, Depart from us. This unclean spirit hated and dreaded Christ, because he knew him to be a Holy One; for the carnal mind is enmity against God, especially against his holiness. When Christ by his grace delivers souls out of the hands of Satan, it is not without tumult in the soul; for that spiteful enemy will disquiet those whom he cannot destroy. This put all who saw it upon considering, What is this new doctrine? A work as great often is wrought now, yet men treat it with contempt and neglect. If this were not so, the conversion of a notorious wicked man to a sober, righteous, and godly life, by the preaching of a crucified Saviour, would cause many to ask, What doctrine is this?
[Mark.1.29-Mark.1.39]
Verses 29-39
Wherever Christ comes, he comes to do good. He cures, that we may minister to him, and to others who are his, and for his sake. Those kept from public ordinances by sickness or other real hinderances, may expect the Saviour's gracious presence; he will soothe their sorrows, and abate their pains. Observe how numerous the patients were. When others speed well with Christ, it should quicken us in seeking after him. Christ departed into a solitary place. Though he was in no danger of distraction, or of temptation to vain-glory, yet he retired. Those who have the most business in public, and of the best kind, must yet sometimes be alone with God.
[Mark.1.40-Mark.1.45]
Verses 40-45
We have here Christ's cleansing of a leper. It teaches us to apply to the Saviour with great humility, and with full submission to his will, saying, "Lord, if thou wilt," without any doubt of Christ's readiness to help the distressed. See also what to expect from Christ; that according to our faith it shall be to us. The poor leper said, If thou wilt. Christ readily wills favours to those who readily refer themselves to his will. Christ would have nothing done that looked like seeking praise of the people. But no reasons now exist why we should hesitate to spread the praises of Christ.

Jesus forgives and heals a paralysed man (verses 1–12)

The man's need to be carried revealed how much suffering human life contains.

The friends who carried him showed real compassion for someone in distress.

Genuine and strong faith may be expressed in different ways, but Jesus receives and approves it.

Sin is the origin of all human suffering and sickness.

To remove the effects decisively, the cause must be dealt with.

Forgiving sin reaches the root of every disease.

Jesus demonstrated his authority to pardon sin through his power to heal the paralysed man.

Physical cures picture the even greater miracle of spiritual healing.

Sin is the soul's disease; when forgiven, it is healed.

When we understand Christ's power to transform sinful souls, we may truly say we have never seen anything like it.

Most people think they are spiritually healthy.

Believing they have no need of a physician, they disregard Christ and the gospel.

But people who have been convicted and humbled, and know there is no hope apart from the Savior, reveal faith by coming to him without delay.

Levi is called and welcomes Jesus (verses 13–17)

Levi, also known as Matthew, was a tax collector serving Rome.

Henry judges that this position was especially discreditable for a Jew of the time, and remarks that honest and fair-dealing publicans were rare.

The occupation reminded Jewish people of their subjection to Rome, leading them to despise its officials.

Yet Jesus called this man to follow him.

Through Christ, God has mercy to pardon the greatest sins and grace to change even those regarded as the greatest sinners.

There is nothing new about good and wise actions being misrepresented and condemned.

Jesus freely ate with tax collectors and people considered sinful, even when Pharisees took offense.

He had come because the world was not righteous.

Without sin, there would have been no occasion for him either to preach repentance or to purchase forgiveness.

We must not form intimate friendships with ungodly people because we love their empty and corrupt conversation.

But we should love their souls and seek their salvation.

Our great Physician has healing power within himself and could not catch the spiritual disease of those he helped.

We, however, can be harmed by bad company.

Therefore, while seeking to help others, we must guard against being led into sin.

The question of fasting (verses 18–22)

Strictly religious people often criticize others merely for failing to conform to all their personal opinions.

Jesus himself was slandered in this way.

We should be willing to endure unjust criticism while carefully avoiding conduct that truly deserves blame.

We must also fulfill every duty at its proper time and in the proper way.

The disciples gather grain on the Sabbath (verses 23–28)

The Sabbath is a holy institution given by God.

It is a privilege and benefit, not forced labor or a burden.

God never intended it to injure human beings.

We must not interpret his command in ways that undermine its own gracious purpose.

The Sabbath was established for humanity living in communities, bearing needs and troubles, and preparing for an everlasting condition of happiness or misery.

Human beings were not created in order to serve the Sabbath, as though keeping it added something to God's own happiness.

They were not commanded to observe it outwardly at the cost of actual harm to themselves.

Every rule connected with its observance must be understood according to mercy.
classic_reading:
[Mark.2.1-Mark.2.12]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Christ heals one sick of the palsy. | (1-12) |
Levi's call, and the entertainment given to Jesus. | (13-17) |
Why Christ's disciples did not fast. | (18-22) |
He justifies his disciples for plucking corn on the sabbath. | (23-28) |
Verses 1-12
It was this man's misery that he needed to be so carried, and shows the suffering state of human life; it was kind of those who so carried him, and teaches the compassion that should be in men, toward their fellow-creatures in distress. True faith and strong faith may work in various ways; but it shall be accepted and approved by Jesus Christ. Sin is the cause of all our pains and sicknesses. The way to remove the effect, is to take away the cause. Pardon of sin strikes at the root of all diseases. Christ proved his power to forgive sin, by showing his power to cure the man sick of the palsy. And his curing diseases was a figure of his pardoning sin, for sin is the disease of the soul; when it is pardoned, it is healed. When we see what Christ does in healing souls, we must own that we never saw the like. Most men think themselves whole; they feel no need of a physician, therefore despise or neglect Christ and his gospel. But the convinced, humbled sinner, who despairs of all help, excepting from the Saviour, will show his faith by applying to him without delay.
[Mark.2.13-Mark.2.17]
Verses 13-17
Matthew was not a good character, or else, being a Jew, he would never have been a publican, that is, a tax-gatherer for the Romans. However, Christ called this publican to follow him. With God, through Christ, there is mercy to pardon the greatest sins, and grace to change the greatest sinners, and make them holy. A faithful, fair-dealing publican was rare. And because the Jews had a particular hatred to an office which proved that they were subject to the Romans, they gave these tax-gatherers an ill name. But such as these our blessed Lord did not hesitate to converse with, when he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh. And it is no new thing for that which is both well done and well designed, to be slandered, and turned to the reproach of the wisest and best of men. Christ would not withdraw, though the Pharisees were offended. If the world had been righteous, there had been no occasion for his coming, either to preach repentance, or to purchase forgiveness. We must not keep company with ungodly men out of love to their vain conversation; but we are to show love to their souls, remembering that our good Physician had the power of healing in himself, and was in no danger of taking the disease; but it is not so with us. In trying to do good to others, let us be careful we do not get harm to ourselves.
[Mark.2.18-Mark.2.22]
Verses 18-22
Strict professors are apt to blame all that do not fully come up to their own views. Christ did not escape slanders; we should be willing to bear them, as well as careful not to deserve them; but should attend to every part of our duty in its proper order and season.
[Mark.2.23-Mark.2.28]
Verses 23-28
The sabbath is a sacred and Divine institution; a privilege and benefit, not a task and drudgery. God never designed it to be a burden to us, therefore we must not make it so to ourselves. The sabbath was instituted for the good of mankind, as living in society, having many wants and troubles, preparing for a state of happiness or misery. Man was not made for the sabbath, as if his keeping it could be of service to God, nor was he commanded to keep it outward observances to his real hurt. Every observance respecting it, is to be interpreted by the rule of mercy.

Jesus heals a withered hand (verses 1–5)

The man's condition was pitiful: a withered hand prevented him from earning his living.

Those unable to help themselves are particularly fitting recipients of practical charity. We should help them.

Stubborn unbelievers may have nothing truthful to say against Christ's teaching, yet refuse to surrender to it.

People notice outward misconduct, but Jesus sees the root of bitterness in the heart, including hardness and blindness.

He was grieved by that inward evil.

Those who refuse repentance should fear the judgment of the One who sees their hearts.

The Sabbath is particularly suitable for acts of mercy. A house of prayer is a suitable place for healing, but the power belongs to Christ, not to either the day or the location.

The gospel's call resembles Jesus' command to stretch out the withered hand.

If people refuse to respond, they remain responsible for refusing the gracious summons.

But if they are healed, all glory belongs to Christ's power and grace.

The crowds come to Jesus (verses 6–12)

Human sickness and suffering ultimately arise from God's just displeasure against sin.

Through Christ's atoning blood, the removal of such troubles—or their transformation into spiritual blessings—has been purchased for believers.

But we should fear the diseases of the soul even more than those of the body.

Christ can heal those spiritual troubles with a single word.

May ever more people press toward him for cleansing and deliverance from their spiritual enemies.

Jesus appoints his apostles (verses 13–21)

Christ calls the people he wills, because grace belongs to him to give.

He summoned the apostles to separate themselves from the crowd, and they came.

He gave them power to heal diseases and cast out demons.

May the Lord continue to send people who have been with him and learned from him to proclaim his gospel as servants of his gracious work.

People whose hearts are fully engaged in God's service can easily endure inconvenience to themselves.

They would rather miss a meal than miss an opportunity to do good.

Those who serve God zealously should expect difficulties caused both by the hatred of enemies and by the mistaken affection of friends.

They must be alert to both.

The scribes accuse Jesus of serving Satan (verses 22–30)

Jesus' doctrine plainly weakened the devil's kingdom.

His expulsion of demons from suffering people demonstrated the same power.

It would make no sense for Satan to support a mission directed against his own dominion.

Christ gave a serious warning about the scribes' blasphemous accusation.

The gospel offers forgiveness through Christ's saving work to even the greatest sinners.

But by this particular sin these opponents would oppose the gifts of the Holy Spirit to be poured out after Christ's ascension.

Such is the hostility of fallen hearts that they may accuse God's servants of doing Satan's work precisely when sinners are being converted and begin living holy lives.

Jesus identifies his true family (verses 31–35)

All genuine Christians have a remarkable comfort.

They are dearer to Christ as his disciples than even merely human ties to a mother, brother or sister could make people, even if those relatives were themselves holy.

The privilege remains available today.

We cannot enjoy Christ's physical presence as his first disciples did, but his spiritual presence is not withheld from us.
classic_reading:
[Mark.3.1-Mark.3.5]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The withered hand healed. | (1-5) |
The people resort to Christ. | (6-12) |
The apostles called. | (13-21) |
The blasphemy of the scribes. | (22-30) |
Christ's relatives. | (31-35) |
Verses 1-5
This man's case was piteous; he had a withered hand, which disabled him from working for his living; and those that are so, are the most proper objects of charity. Let those be helped that cannot help themselves. But stubborn infidels, when they can say nothing against the truth, yet will not yield. We hear what is said amiss, and see what is done amiss; but Christ looks at the root of bitterness in the heart, the blindness and hardness of that, and is grieved. Let hard-hearted sinners tremble to think of the anger with which he will look upon them shortly, when the day of his wrath comes. The great healing day now is the sabbath, and the healing place the house of prayer; but the healing power is of Christ. The gospel command is like that recorded here: though our hands are withered, yet, if we will not stretch them out, it is our own fault that we are not healed. But if we are healed, Christ, his power and grace, must have all the glory.
[Mark.3.6-Mark.3.12]
Verses 6-12
All our sicknesses and calamities spring from the anger of God against our sins. Their removal, or the making them blessings to us, was purchased to us by the blood of Christ. But the plagues and diseases of our souls, of our hearts, are chiefly to be dreaded; and He can heal them also by a word. May more and more press to Christ to be healed of these plagues, and to be delivered from the enemies of their souls.
[Mark.3.13-Mark.3.21]
Verses 13-21
Christ calls whom he will; for his grace is his own. He had called the apostles to separate themselves from the crowd, and they came unto him. He now gave them power to heal sicknesses, and to cast out devils. May the Lord send forth more and more of those who have been with him, and have learned of him to preach his gospel, to be instruments in his blessed work. Those whose hearts are enlarged in the work of God, can easily bear with what is inconvenient to themselves, and will rather lose a meal than an opportunity of doing good. Those who go on with zeal in the work of God, must expect hinderances, both from the hatred of enemies, and mistaken affections of friends, and need to guard against both.
[Mark.3.22-Mark.3.30]
Verses 22-30
It was plain that the doctrine of Christ had a direct tendency to break the devil's power; and it was as plain, that casting of him out of the bodies of people, confirmed that doctrine; therefore Satan could not support such a design. Christ gave an awful warning against speaking such dangerous words. It is true the gospel promises, because Christ has purchased, forgiveness for the greatest sins and sinners; but by this sin, they would oppose the gifts of the Holy Ghost after Christ's ascension. Such is the enmity of the heart, that unconverted men pretend believers are doing Satan's work, when sinners are brought to repentance and newness of life.
[Mark.3.31-Mark.3.35]
Verses 31-35
It is a great comfort to all true Christians, that they are dearer to Christ than mother, brother, or sister as such, merely as relations in the flesh would have been, even had they been holy. Blessed be God, this great and gracious privilege is ours even now; for though Christ's bodily presence cannot be enjoyed by us, his spiritual presence is not denied us.

The sower and the soils (verses 1–20)

This parable contains teaching so important that everyone capable of hearing should pay attention.

If we do not understand the plain truths of the gospel, how will we understand its deeper teachings?

Considering the unhappy condition of people without gospel privileges should make Christ's disciples value those privileges more highly.

In the church's great field, God's word is announced widely.

But relatively few hearers receive it in a way that produces lasting fruit.

Many feel moved or enthusiastic for a time yet receive no enduring benefit.

The reason the word leaves so little permanent impression is that their hearts have not been prepared to receive it.

The devil is especially active among careless hearers, like birds eating seed left exposed on a path.

Many continue in a barren religious profession until they perish.

Shallow religious feelings cannot endure.

Many neglect the work of the heart, without which religion has no true substance.

Others are hindered by an abundance of worldly concerns and possessions.

But people who own little can also be ruined by giving themselves over to bodily indulgence.

God rightly expects fruit from everyone privileged to hear his gospel.

This includes a renewed disposition, Christian graces exercised each day and duties faithfully performed.

Ask the Lord, through his new-creating grace, to make our hearts good soil.

May his word produce good words and works through Jesus Christ, bringing glory to God the Father.

The lamp and the growing seed (verses 21–34)

Jesus taught these parables to call his disciples' full attention to his word.

Through learning from him, they would become able to teach others.

A lamp is lit to illuminate a room, not to be hidden beneath a container.

Likewise, disciples receive light in order to help others.

The growing seed pictures how God's kingdom advances.

When Christ's word occupies its rightful place in a soul, the change becomes visible through good conduct.

Growth is gradual: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.

Once genuine spiritual life has begun, it advances.

The first work of grace may seem like a very small beginning.

Even while it is still growing it produces significant blessings.

How much greater will its glory be when that work is perfected in heaven!

Jesus calms the storm (verses 35–41)

Jesus slept during the storm to test his disciples' faith and move them to pray.

Their faith was weak, but their prayers were urgent.

When our sinful hearts resemble a restless sea and our passions become unruly, let us hear Christ's command: “Be silent! Be still!”

When we experience outward conflict and inward fear, and our spirits are overwhelmed, one word from him can bring an immediate, great calm.

Jesus asked why they were so frightened.

A hard heart can be softened, spiritual diseases can be healed, and people conscious of their weakness can persevere to the end.

Those who grieve over unbelief should seek Christ's grace to overcome it.

His grace is sufficient.

Everyone Christ heals is healed effectively.

Satan does not leave willingly those whom he has enslaved for a long time.

When he can no longer deceive or destroy someone, he may still attempt to fill the soul with fear and turmoil.

The disciples must not assume every task in Christ's service will be equally easy.

Some difficult work requires more than ordinary effort.

Jesus corrects the apostles' pride and intolerance (verses 30–40)

Jesus' suffering was approaching.

It would be terrible for even demons to treat him in such a way.

It is all the more astonishing that human beings should abuse the Son of Man who came to redeem them.

But Christ never spoke of his death without also speaking of his resurrection, which would remove his disgrace and should have lessened the disciples' sorrow.

Many people remain ignorant because they are ashamed to ask questions.

Jesus explained his love and grace clearly, but the disciples still struggled to understand.

We will have to answer for our speech and discussions, especially arguments about which of us deserves the greatest honor.

People most humble and self-denying resemble Christ most closely and will receive his warmest approval.

Jesus illustrated this with a child: welcoming such a child in Christ's name is welcoming Christ himself.

The disciples wanted to silence a person who was successfully helping sinners through the name of Jesus but was not working with their own group.

People today can make the same mistake.

Jesus corrected them.

Anyone truly bringing sinners to repentance, faith in Christ and holy conduct is demonstrating that the Lord is at work.

We should not reject genuine gospel service merely because the minister belongs to another circle of disciples.

Sin is worse than suffering (verses 41–50)

Jesus repeatedly spoke of the wicked person's worm that never dies and fire that is never extinguished.

Henry understands the never-dying worm as the remorse of conscience and painful self-awareness that persist in judgment.

Enduring severe hardship, suffering and self-denial during this short life is immeasurably better than enjoying every worldly pleasure for a time and suffering eternally afterward.

Like offerings presented in sacrifice, we must be seasoned with salt.

Our sinful desires and inclinations must be subdued and put to death by the Holy Spirit.

People who possess the salt of grace should show that a living principle of grace truly governs their hearts.

It will drive out corrupt tendencies that offend God or trouble their consciences.

[Mark.9.1-Mark.9.13]
Chapter 9
Chapter Outline
The transfiguration. | (1-13) |
An evil spirit cast out. | (14-29) |
The apostles reproved. | (30-40) |
Pain to be preferred to sin. | (41-50) |
Verses 1-13
Here is a prediction of the near approach Christ's kingdom. A glimpse of that kingdom was given in the transfiguration of Christ. It is good to be away from the world, and alone with Christ: and how good to be with Christ glorified in heaven with all the saints! But when it is well with us, we are apt not to care for others, and in the fulness of our enjoyments, we forget the many wants of our brethren. God owns Jesus, and accepts him as his beloved Son, and is ready to accept us in him. Therefore we must own and accept him as our beloved Saviour, and must give up ourselves to be ruled by him. Christ does not leave the soul, when joys and comforts leave it. Jesus explained to the disciples the prophecy about Elias. This was very suitable to the ill usage of John Baptist.
[Mark.9.14-Mark.9.29]
Verses 14-29
The father of the suffering youth reflected on the want of power in the disciples; but Christ will have him reckon the disappointment to the want of faith. Very much is promised to our believing. If thou canst believe, it is possible that thy hard heart may be softened, thy spiritual diseases may be cured; and, weak as thou art, thou mayest be able to hold out to the end. Those that complain of unbelief, must look up to Christ for grace to help them against it, and his grace will be sufficient for them. Whom Christ cures, he cures effectually. But Satan is unwilling to be driven from those that have been long his slaves, and, when he cannot deceive or destroy the sinner, he will cause him all the terror that he can. The disciples must not think to do their work always with the same ease; some services call for more than ordinary pains.
[Mark.9.30-Mark.9.40]
Verses 30-40
The time of Christ's suffering drew nigh. Had he been delivered into the hands of devils, and they had done this, it had not been so strange; but that men should thus shamefully treat the Son of man, who came to redeem and save them, is wonderful. Still observe that when Christ spake of his death, he always spake of his resurrection, which took the reproach of it from himself, and should have taken the grief of it from his disciples. Many remain ignorant because they are ashamed to inquire. Alas! that while the Saviour teaches so plainly the things which belong to his love and grace, men are so blinded that they understand not his sayings. We shall be called to account about our discourses, and to account for our disputes, especially about being greater than others. Those who are most humble and self-denying, most resemble Christ, and shall be most tenderly owned by him. This Jesus taught them by a sign; whoever shall receive one like this child, receives me. Many have been like the disciples, ready to silence men who have success in preaching to sinners repentance in Christ's name, because they follow not with them. Our Lord blamed the apostles, reminding them that he who wrought miracles in his name would not be likely to hurt his cause. If sinners are brought to repent, to believe in the Saviour, and to live sober, righteous, and godly lives, we then see that the Lord works by the preacher.
[Mark.9.41-Mark.9.50]
Verses 41-50
It is repeatedly said of the wicked, Their worm dieth not, as well as, The fire is never quenched. Doubtless, remorse of conscience and keen self-reflection are this never-dying worm. Surely it is beyond compare better to undergo all possible pain, hardship, and self-denial here, and to be happy for ever hereafter, than to enjoy all kinds of worldly pleasure for a season, and to be miserable for ever. Like the sacrifices, we must be salted with salt; our corrupt affections must be subdued and mortified by the Holy Spirit. Those that have the salt of grace, must show they have a living principle of grace in their hearts, which works out corrupt dispositions in the soul that would offend God, or our own consciences.

Jesus speaks about divorce (verses 1–12)

Wherever Jesus went, people gathered to hear his teaching.

Preaching was his constant practice.

Jesus explained that Moses permitted divorce because of human hardness of heart.

That is hardly a reason to use the permission casually.

God himself joined man and woman together and fitted them to be companions, comforts and helpers to one another.

The bond God established should not be dissolved lightly.

Anyone eager to send away a spouse should consider what it would be like if God dealt with that person in the same way.

Jesus receives children (verses 13–16)

Parents and caregivers brought small children to Jesus so that he would touch and bless them.

The text gives no indication they were ill or needed bodily healing.

They may not even have been old enough to understand formal instruction.

Yet those responsible for them believed Christ's blessing would benefit their souls, so they brought them.

Jesus commanded that the children be allowed to come and that no one hinder them.

As soon as children can understand the Savior's words, they should be taught to come to him.

Adults must likewise receive God's kingdom as children receive care and instruction from parents, caregivers and teachers.

Jesus and the wealthy young man (verses 17–22)

The young ruler was earnest and wanted to know what he should do now to obtain eternal happiness.

Most people ask only for this life's pleasures and advantages (Psalm 4:6).

He sought good conduct here so he could obtain the highest good in the coming life.

Jesus helped his understanding and directed his conduct.

But the encounter ended in sorrow.

The man wanted to know what more he needed to do for eternal life.

Jesus tested whether he truly valued that life enough to bear a present cross for a future crown.

The young man wanted to follow Christ without giving up the wealth he loved.

He left in grief because he could not hold on to both ultimate treasures.

No one can serve both God and wealth (Matthew 6:24).

Wealth as an obstacle (verses 23–31)

Jesus explained the great danger facing those who possess abundant worldly goods.

People determined to acquire more wealth rarely appreciate Christ and his grace properly.

He also taught about the great salvation belonging to those with few possessions who nevertheless give up what they have for him.

One of a godly person's hardest trials is surrendering attachment even to dear friends and relatives when love for Jesus requires it.

Even people who gain immeasurably through Christ must still expect to suffer for him until reaching heaven.

Let those with little learn contentment.

Let those with much watch against love of wealth.

We should ask for grace to surrender everything if Christ requires it and to use faithfully everything we are permitted to keep.

Jesus foretells suffering and teaches humble service (verses 32–45)

Christ's persistent determination to finish the saving work assigned to him astonished his disciples and should continue to astonish us.

Worldly honor is attractive, and even Jesus' own disciples were repeatedly dazzled by it.

We need wisdom and grace to know how to suffer with him.

We may trust him to determine how much heavenly glory he will give us.

Jesus explained that worldly rulers commonly abuse their authority.

If he granted every request we make, our motives would soon reveal desire for fame, rank and power, along with unwillingness to drink from his cup or share his baptism of suffering.

Sometimes receiving exactly what we ask would ruin us.

But Christ loves his people and gives them only what is good for them.

Bartimaeus receives sight (verses 46–52)

Bartimaeus had heard about Christ's miracles.

When he learned that Jesus was nearby, he hoped to regain his sight.

Those seeking Christ's healing should recognize him as the promised Messiah.

His gracious invitation encourages us to believe that those who come to him will receive the help they truly need.

We must put aside the garment of self-sufficiency.

Like someone casting off a long garment that might hinder running, we should lay aside every weight and the sin that clings most closely to us (Hebrews 12:1).

Bartimaeus asked that his eyes might be opened.

The ability to work and earn one's bread is a real gift.

People given healthy bodies and senses should not make themselves practically disabled through foolishness or idleness.

Jesus restored his sight.

His words pointed to Bartimaeus's faith in the Son of David, in Christ's pity and power—not merely to repeated words or cries.

Jesus himself moved that faith into action.

When gospel preaching or Christian Scripture comes within reach, Christ is passing by.

That is our opportunity to come to him.

But spiritual healing is not the end of our duty.

When Christ opens our eyes, we should continue following him, learning from his teaching and honoring him in our lives.

People with spiritual sight recognize such beauty in Christ that they desire to follow eagerly.

[Mark.10.1-Mark.10.12]
Chapter 10
Chapter Outline
The Pharisees' question concerning divorce. | (1-12) |
Christ's love to little children. | (13-16) |
Christ's discourse with the rich young man. | (17-22) |
The hinderance of riches. | (23-31) |
Christ foretells his sufferings. | (32-45) |
Bartimeus healed. | (46-52) |
Verses 1-12
Wherever Jesus was, the people flocked after him in crowds, and he taught them. Preaching was Christ's constant practice. He here shows that the reason why Moses' law allowed divorce, was such that they ought not to use the permission; it was only for the hardness of their hearts. God himself joined man and wife together; he has fitted them to be comforts and helps for each other. The bond which God has tied, is not to be lightly untied. Let those who are for putting away their wives consider what would become of themselves, if God should deal with them in like manner.
[Mark.10.13-Mark.10.16]
Verses 13-16
Some parents or nurses brought little children to Christ, that he should touch them, in token of his blessing them. It does not appear that they needed bodily cures, nor were they capable of being taught: but those who had the care of them believed that Christ's blessing would do their souls good; therefore they brought them to him. Jesus ordered that they should be brought to him, and that nothing should be said or done to hinder it. Children should be directed to the Saviour as soon as they are able to understand his words. Also, we must receive the kingdom of God as little children; we must stand affected to Christ and his grace, as little children to their parents, nurses, and teachers.
[Mark.10.17-Mark.10.22]
Verses 17-22
This young ruler showed great earnestness. He asked what he should do now, that he might be happy for ever. Most ask for good to be had in this world; any good, [Ps.4.6] Psa 4:6; he asks for good to be done in this world, in order to enjoy the greatest good in the other world. Christ encouraged this address by assisting his faith, and by directing his practice. But here is a sorrowful parting between Jesus and this young man. He asks Christ what he shall do more than he has done, to obtain eternal life; and Christ puts it to him, whether he has indeed that firm belief of, and that high value for eternal life which he seems to have. Is he willing to bear a present cross, in expectation of future crown? The young man was sorry he could not be a follower of Christ upon easier terms; that he could not lay hold on eternal life, and keep hold of his worldly possessions too. He went away grieved. See [Matt.6.24] Mt 6:24, Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
[Mark.10.23-Mark.10.31]
Verses 23-31
Christ took this occasion to speak to his disciples about the difficulty of the salvation of those who have abundance of this world. Those who thus eagerly seek the wealth of the world, will never rightly prize Christ and his grace. Also, as to the greatness of the salvation of those who have but little of this world, and leave it for Christ. The greatest trial of a good man's constancy is, when love to Jesus calls him to give up love to friends and relatives. Even when gainers by Christ, let them still expect to suffer for him, till they reach heaven. Let us learn contentment in a low state, and to watch against the love of riches in a high one. Let us pray to be enabled to part with all, if required, in Christ's service, and to use all we are allowed to keep in his service.
[Mark.10.32-Mark.10.45]
Verses 32-45
Christ's going on with his undertaking for the salvation of mankind, was, is, and will be, the wonder of all his disciples. Worldly honour is a glittering thing, with which the eyes of Christ's own disciples have many times been dazzled. Our care must be, that we may have wisdom and grace to know how to suffer with him; and we may trust him to provide what the degrees of our glory shall be. Christ shows them that dominion was generally abused in the world. If Jesus would gratify all our desires, it would soon appear that we desire fame or authority, and are unwilling to taste of his cup, or to have his baptism; and should often be ruined by having our prayers answered. But he loves us, and will only give his people what is good for them.
[Mark.10.46-Mark.10.52]
Verses 46-52
Bartimeus had heard of Jesus and his miracles, and learning that he was passing by, hoped to recover his eyesight. In coming to Christ for help and healing, we should look to him as the promised Messiah. The gracious calls Christ gives us to come to him, encourage our hope, that if we come to him we shall have what we come for. Those who would come to Jesus, must cast away the garment of their own sufficiency, must free themselves from every weight, and the sin that, like long garments, most easily besets them, [Heb.12.1] He 12:1. He begged that his eyes might be opened. It is very desirable to be able to earn our bread; and where God has given men limbs and senses, it is a shame, by foolishness and slothfulness, to make themselves, in effect, blind and lame. His eyes were opened. Thy faith has made thee whole: faith in Christ as the Son of David, and in his pity and power; not thy repeated words, but thy faith; Christ setting thy faith to work. Let sinners be exhorted to imitate blind Bartimeus. Where the gospel is preached, or the written words of truth circulated, Jesus is passing by, and this is the opportunity. It is not enough to come to Christ for spiritual healing, but, when we are healed, we must continue to follow him; that we may honour him, and receive instruction from him. Those who have spiritual eyesight, see that beauty in Christ which will draw them to run after him.
